## Appendix A. Taught contracts: the author-facing index
- V10 The build pipeline enforces structure.
- V11 It checks declarations, wiring, types and conformance.
- V12 A residue of semantic facts remains that no check can enforce.
- V13 A component or periphery author who knows them writes code that comes out right, and so does a service user, who writes conditions, trim problems, taps and linearization calls.
- V14 An author who does not produces defensive delays, duplicated math or mistimed samples, and no diagnostic fires anywhere.
- V15 The IMU's boundary-sampling note (§8.6) is the archetype. [§8.6]
- V16 This appendix is an index, not a second home.
- V17 Each contract gets one recall line here, and its normative statement stays in the owning section.
- V18 That applies the one-home-per-datum rule to the document itself.
- V19 The index has three groups, for component authors, for periphery authors and consumers, and for service users.
- V20 For component authors:
- V21 The stage funnel (§5.2, §5.3; D-341). [§5.2, §5.3, D-341] (bold)
- V22 The stage name at its tier (the continuous or discrete side) fixes the maximal legal view set.
- V23 The component's declarations narrow that set to the bundle.
- V24 The signature's destructuring narrows the bundle to the actual reads.
- V25 In short, stage name at its tier ⊇ bundle ⊇ destructured reads.
- V26 So "no `direct` in the name" is the no-feedthrough property.
- V27 The teaching line runs as follows.
- V28 Stage 1 publishes what you know from state alone.
- V29 Stage 2 adds what needs inputs.
- V30 Your dynamics read your own published results instead of recomputing them.
- V31 One home per datum (§5.2; D-035). [§5.2, D-035] (bold)
- V32 The signal table holds produced signals only, never transported ones (§4.3). [§4.3]
- V33 The buffer holds `x`, the `s` and `m` stores hold `s` and `m`, and the table holds signals.
- V34 No store mirrors another.
- V35 The value-level constructor (§8.2; D-139). [§8.2, D-139] (bold)
- V36 A field-emitting component ships the map from (component, input values) to handle as a plain public function, and its output stage merely calls it.
- V37 The condition math (§14.1) must be able to produce the sweep's exact handle outside any sweep. [§14.1]
- V38 Only the component's author can write that function without re-creating the drift class.
- V39 Boundary sampling (§10.5/§10.6; worked example §8.6; D-056). [§10.5, §10.6, §8.6, D-056] (bold)
- V40 "Sampling at `t_k`" means sampling the post-integration, post-projection, stage-1-fresh state.
- V41 A due tick's gated stages run inside the boundary sweep and sample the completed boundary.
- V42 An author who distrusts that guarantee, with a defensive one-tick delay or a re-derivation inside the sampler, silently degrades the model.
- V43 The startup hole (§10.5, §14.5; D-205). [§10.5, §14.5, D-205] (bold)
- V44 An offset component's first tick is at `Φ·Δt_base`, where `Φ` is its phase in base ticks and `Δt_base` the base tick period.
- V45 Until then its cells hold what it published at boundary zero (the initialization boundary at `t₀`).
- V46 Its output stages still run at `t₀`, evaluated from the authored world.
- V47 A startup hole, a component dark until its first tick, is a modeling decision.
- V48 The author spells it as a validity flag or a mode, and the framework withholds no publication by default.
- V49 Interval alignment (§14.5; D-067, D-273). [§14.5, D-067, D-273] (bold)
- V50 A boundary's `s_update` is the outgoing transition.
- V51 At tick `t_k` it consumes the completed boundary's samples and produces `s_{k+1}`, the value the component's next tick decodes.
- V52 That is the sampled-data `z⁻¹` delay, by construction.
- V53 Hence `s_update` runs at boundary zero.
- V54 That run is the `t₀` sample's only chance.
- V55 The same placement fixes what a discrete store holds at rest.
- V56 After any boundary the store holds the state the component's next due tick decodes, and its cell holds the sample its last tick published.
- V57 A counter due at boundary zero and authored at 0 holds 1 after `init!` alone.
- V58 A discrete store copied off a stopped run into a condition therefore starts that component one tick ahead.
- V59 A state what-if goes through `overlay!` instead, which writes the condition onto the stopped run's own stores and continues the run, with an overlaid discrete store as the next tick's state, so no copy through a condition and `init!` is needed (§12.6, D-429). [§12.6, D-429]
- V60 Same-tick reset consumption (§5.3; D-089), on the discrete tier. [§5.3, D-089] (bold)
- V61 A commanded reset of a discrete component's `s` is an input.
- V62 For same-tick output semantics the output stage consumes that input, overriding the state-derived path, and `s_update` stores the matching `s⁺`.
- V63 A reset honored only in `s_update` reaches the outputs one tick late, and the plant integrates a full step under the stale command.
- V64 Both spellings are legal, and they mean different things.
- V65 The continuous tier has no such choice (next entry).
- V66 Continuous-tier resets (§3.1, §10.6, §5.3; D-141). [§3.1, §10.6, §5.3, D-141] (bold)
- V67 A continuous component's state reset is an event.
- V68 Only handlers write `x`.
- V69 So even a commanded reset, where the condition arrives as an ordinary `Bool` input (weight-on-wheels is the shipped instance), is spelled as an event whose guard reads that input.
- V70 The discrete tier's input spelling does not transfer.
- V71 The reason is semantic, not stylistic.
- V72 Only the discrete tier's update stage is already a jump map, so a reset there is just another value for `s⁺`.
- V73 A continuous state jump, by contrast, must be solver-visible and applied between integration segments.
- V74 Every hybrid tool converges on that flow/jump split.
- V75 Simulink applies its reset ports through zero-crossing events plus a solver restart, and Modelica's `reinit` is syntactically legal only inside a `when`.
- V76 There is no stale-output hazard to manage either.
- V77 §10.6 re-sweeps outputs to quiescence after handlers, so a continuous edge-reset is same-boundary by construction. [§10.6]
- V78 Undeclared modes (§3.1, §2.3; D-345, D-179). [§3.1, §2.3, D-345, D-179] (bold)
- V79 A branch in the flow that switches on a continuous quantity, such as an integrator that stops accumulating once its output reaches a limit, is a mode change with no declared event.
- V80 It switches inside a step, at no boundary and against no prior, so nothing localizes it and nothing records it.
- V81 Such a switch is spelled as a mode moved by an event, or as a branch on another component's mode-derived output, which changes only when that component's events fire.
- V82 Guard predicates, edges and priors (§2.3, §10.4, §10.6; D-365). [§2.3, §10.4, §10.6, D-365] (bold)
- V83 A guard defines a predicate, either as a `Bool` or as a sign value `σ`, which holds when `σ ≥ 0`.
- V84 The form chosen is the detection policy.
- V85 A `Bool` guard is boundary-detected, a sign guard is localized.
- V86 Boundary detection is exact only for a guard over modes, root inputs and held discrete outputs.
- V87 A guard reading an input fed by continuous state or by time can cross inside a step.
- V88 Events fire on edges from not-holding to holding, judged against per-event priors, where the prior is the previous boundary's quiescent sample.
- V89 A predicate that keeps holding fires once, at the boundary where it first held.
- V90 Boundary zero sets every prior to not-holding, so a predicate already holding in the authored state fires at `t₀`.
- V91 The opposite crossing direction is a second event with the negated guard.
- V92 Latching and release pairs (§10.4, §10.6; D-290, D-181). [§10.4, §10.6, D-290, D-181] (bold)
- V93 A release predicate, such as "the input points back into the range", does not hold at an input of exactly zero, but the sign form `-u` alone holds there.
- V94 It gates on the strict comparison instead, as `u < 0 ? -u : -one(u)` or as the `Bool` form `u < 0`.
- V95 The predicate that latches the mode stays ungated on it.
- V96 Gated on the free mode, each handler hands the other guard a fresh edge, and the boundary chatters until the firing budget breaks the tie, under a `FiringBudget` warning.
- V97 Handler-phase visibility (§5.3, §10.6; D-154). [§5.3, §10.6, D-154] (bold)
- V98 A handler executes against exactly the world its guard fired on.
- V99 Its own `y`, foreign `u` and its own `x`/`m` all come from the firing round's sweep.
- V100 A component fires at most one event per round.
- V101 Its later own events are re-decided against the next round's sweep, one round per causal link, within and across components alike.
- V102 Only sweeps write the signal table.
- V103 Stage totality (§9.3; §13.4, §13.5; D-142). [§9.3, §13.4, §13.5, D-142] (bold)
- V104 Stage code is total over type-valid inputs.
- V105 The probe evaluates every user function against values chosen for their types alone.
- V106 A value-level throw is a build failure there and a `StepError` at runtime.
- V107 Physical plausibility is a published stop request.
- V108 Self-consistency asserts belong in tests.
- V109 Parameter validation belongs at instance construction, not inside a stage.
- V110 Stop-request sampling (§13.5; D-316). [§13.5, D-316] (bold)
- V111 Stop requests are read in completed-boundary snapshots (the immutable per-boundary publications).
- V112 Declare a sign-form (localized) event if the stop needs localizing.
- V113 Every request stops the run unless the advance ignores it.
- V114 Never cache `Δt` (§10.5; D-019, D-291). [§10.5, D-019, D-291] (bold)
- V115 An author must never store `Δt`, or any `Δt`-derived coefficient, as a component parameter.
- V116 The discretized law reads `Δt` from the bundle and recomputes its derived coefficients per tick, which costs a few arithmetic operations.
- V117 Under scoped multipliers a component author cannot know the absolute rate, which does not exist until composition.
- V118 A discretized law is written to be stable at every period a deployment may assign, since the component cannot know its period at construction and no check compares the law against it.
- V119 No mutable cache in a field handle (§4.4, §4.1; D-344). [§4.4, §4.1, D-344] (bold)
- V120 A field handle must hold no mutable cache, such as a memoizing interpolator or a lazy loader.
- V121 Concurrent consumers and the GUI thread would race on it.
- V122 The remedy is to restructure the interpolant to be pure.
- V123 The rule is the author's, because the build does not look inside a field handle.
- V124 The bulk data a handle references stays read-only for the duration of the run.
- V125 Contracts by type (§8.1, §9.7; D-297). [§8.1, §9.7, D-297] (bold)
- V126 A leaf's contract declarations must be determined by the component's type, its type parameters included, and never by its field values.
- V127 Those declarations are `u_types`, `y_types` and `state_events`, and the shapes of `x_init`/`s_init`/`m_init`.
- V128 A contract that genuinely varies takes a type parameter, as `SumJunction{V, N}` and `Or{N}` do.
- V129 `ws_init` is the one exception.
- V130 The build reads each declaration once, against the concrete instance, so a value-dependent contract does not announce itself.
- V131 This is a rule authors keep, not a check the build can run.
- V132 Deliberate stripping (§13.7, §14.10, §9.5; D-266). [§13.7, §14.10, §9.5, D-266] (bold)
- V133 `Freeze` strips partials, and its wire then declares a zero coupling in every Jacobian along that path.
- V134 That is a modeling decision, stated on the page rather than buried mid-expression.
- V135 Stripping mid-expression at a leaf left unpinned remains legal and remains unseen.
- V136 A sampler is no substitute, because it changes the model, holding the value between ticks.
- V137 Where the coupling matters to the Jacobian, a component keeps its input entry tolerant and supplies its own local derivative inside the stage.
- V138 A gain scheduled from seeded state carries the schedule's partials into the Jacobian like any other wired input, and a model that wants it held at its nominal value routes it through `Freeze`.
- V139 The unit delay's tier caveat (§5.5, §13.7; D-348). [§5.5, §13.7, D-348] (bold)
- V140 A unit delay is a modeling decision, not a transparent wire, because the delayed signal is genuinely sampled.
- V141 Inserting a `UnitDelay` into a continuous loop moves that signal onto the discrete tier and inserts a `Δt_base`-scale zero-order hold into the model's mathematics.
- V142 The cycle diagnostic therefore says so rather than offering the remedy as free.
- V143 Unwired contributors (§6.2; D-084, D-323, D-037). [§6.2, D-084, D-323, D-037] (bold)
- V144 A summing junction makes its own bookkeeping loud.
- V145 A contributor it counts but nobody wires is an unconnected-input error.
- V146 A contributor's output that nobody wires stays legal and silent, as any unconnected output does.
- V147 Every contribution a total includes is a declared wire, so an unwired contributor drops out of the total and no diagnostic fires.
- V148 Fold order is the positional order of the junction's inputs.
- V149 Reassigning contributors to different inputs changes summation order, hence bits.
- V150 For periphery authors and consumers:
- V151 Levels, never deltas (§11.4; D-024). [§11.4, D-024] (bold)
- V152 Staged input values are levels (`press_count = 17`, never `presses += 1`), which makes them idempotent under coalescing.
- V153 Button edges ride as monotonic counters.
- V154 Cross-datum state such as press counters and edge detection lives in the device struct.
- V155 The loop maintains it, and it arrives inside the datum, because `map_input` is pure (§11.6). [§11.6]
- V156 The device loop idioms (§11.6, §12.4; D-373). [§11.6, §12.4, D-373] (bold)
- V157 Loop on `running(handle)`.
- V158 Make every blocking call interruptible, through an `unblock!` override or timeouts.
- V159 Voluntary exit is returning.
- V160 There are three canonical shapes.
- V161 Timer-poll sleeps, polls and stages.
- V162 Source-driven blocks on your socket, and `unblock!` closes it.
- V163 Boundary-driven calls `wait_next_snapshot`, gathers and sends.
- V164 A forgotten predicate check surfaces as `DeviceJoinTimeout` with your device's name.
- V165 A stall surfaces as a stale heartbeat.
- V166 `shutdown!` closes only what is open (§11.6, §12.4; D-268). [§11.6, §12.4, D-268] (bold)
- V167 The framework runs `shutdown!` on every exit path, including your own `init!`'s failure.
- V168 A throw half-way through acquisition hands the half-built device straight back to you.
- V169 So guard each release (`isopen`, a `nothing` handle) rather than assuming initialization completed.
- V170 You do not carry the converse burden.
- V171 `init!` owes no cleanup of its own.
- V172 An operator interrupt (Ctrl-C in an interactive session) can repeat a `shutdown!` call, and it can release a device whose `init!` never began.
- V173 The same tolerance covers both calls, and neither is reported.
- V174 Binding traits are declarations, mappings are your own idiom (§11.6, D-382). [§11.6, D-382] (bold)
- V175 Keep `is_input`/`is_output`/`is_greedy` trivial, a literal or a flag read off a field fixed at the constructor call.
- V176 The framework reads them only during `attach!`, and cross-checks each against the enumeration method it implies.
- V177 `map_input`/`map_output` are a different kind of thing.
- V178 They are conventions of the loop idiom, called only by your own `loop` and never by the framework.
- V179 The names are worth keeping for readers, and nothing enforces them.
- V180 Bad datum vs. bug (§11.6, §13.4; D-105). [§11.6, §13.4, D-105] (bold)
- V181 Catch what your parser can throw, call `report!(handle, MalformedDatum(cause))`, stage nothing and continue.
- V182 Let everything else propagate, and the wrapper makes it `DeviceCrash`.
- V183 Tolerating everything hides bugs as "device attached, nothing happens".
- V184 Tolerating nothing kills a live link on its first truncated datagram.
- V185 Derived liveness (§11.7; D-045). [§11.7, D-045] (bold)
- V186 A widget is live iff its port's feed chain terminates in a root input inside the GUI's own claim in the run's frozen partition.
- V187 There is no per-port marking, and unexported ports are unpokeable.
- V188 The two observation sides (§11.2, §13.5, §14.2, §14.7; D-414, D-065). [§11.2, §13.5, §14.2, §14.7, D-414, D-065] (bold)
- V189 A deep snapshot path is an inspection read.
- V190 It sees everything and promises nothing across builds (§13.3). [§13.3]
- V191 An exported output face is an integration read.
- V192 It carries curated, writer-independent meaning, and it is the only shield against silent semantic drift.
- V193 Bind faces in anything meant to outlive the current build.
- V194 The store selectors (`get_state`/`get_deriv`) belong to neither side.
- V195 They read live stores, never snapshots (the source rule, §14.4). [§14.4]
- V196 A service user's path, in a condition, a trim read or a tap, may reach any depth.
- V197 No check refuses a deep path past a generically held field (one held through a non-concrete field type).
- V198 Ownership alone is convention, so keeping a deep path inside an owned subtree is idiomatic rather than machine-checked.
- V199 An equilibrium equation meant to survive substitution at a generic seam (a narrow, named interface) reads a face.
- V200 Publications, not frames (§12.3, §10.4; D-028, D-230). [§12.3, §10.4, D-028, D-230] (bold)
- V201 The boundary counter behind the next-snapshot wait counts published boundaries, that is grid, `t` (an event's crossing instant inside a step) and boundary zero, not frames.
- V202 Consecutive wakes are therefore not necessarily `h` apart.
- V203 A slow consumer skips boundaries and always receives the current world.
- V204 A snapshot carries the trajectory's published-boundary ordinal with `t`, so any holder of a snapshot indexes it without consulting the loop.
- V205 A new trajectory restarts the ordinal at zero.
- V206 The counter is never reset across trajectories, and its absolute value is nowhere normative.
- V207 Conditioning upstream, aircraft semantics in-model (§11.4; D-045). [§11.4, D-045] (bold)
- V208 Mappings are binding data, not shaping code.
- V209 A mapping is a declarative table from axis or button to root input, with per-axis conditioning parameters such as deadzone and expo strength.
- V210 A face's meaning is writer-independent, so faces carry post-conditioning semantics.
- V211 A GUI slider or a script writes the same command a curved stick delivers.
- V212 That GUI-parity test places conditioning upstream.
- V213 Aircraft-semantic derivation must not ride along.
- V214 A command fan-out is the case in point.
- V215 It is flight control system design and lives in-model.
- V216 For service users:
- V217 Post-commit trim checks (§14.7, §14.9; D-262, D-139, D-417). [§14.7, §14.9, D-262, D-139, D-417] (bold)
- V218 Under analytic elimination, the condition math pins the state from the targets and the atmosphere the user's `params` record holds, while the world measures against the atmosphere the baseline wrote.
- V219 If the two disagree, the residuals vanish at a true equilibrium that is not the requested point, and nothing in the residual system can tell.
- V220 The service reports checks once, at the committed state, and never solves them.
- V221 A check reading EAS from the world's airdata, minus the requested value, is where a world measurement meets the request.
- V222 A check earns its place only on a quantity the world measures by itself, and on one the condition writes directly it is always zero.
- V223 The problem receives the environment and never writes it.
- V224 The held discrete tier (§14.10, §14.7, §14.8, §8.2; D-213, D-063). [§14.10, §14.7, §14.8, §8.2, D-213, D-063] (bold)
- V225 Trim and linearization differentiate the continuous dynamics with the discrete state held.
- V226 A frozen discrete output is a constant with zero partials, and for that question it is the exact answer.
- V227 Differentiating through the discrete side means differentiating a different object, the sampled-data step map, which is recorded, not built.
- V228 The services hold the discrete tier through the solve, so a controller's stores are not decisions.
- V229 The values that keep a closed loop at rest, such as each integrator's trim value, are the author's to derive and write into the condition.
- V230 What-if replay from `init!` (§12.7; D-274). [§12.7, D-274] (bold)
- V231 Replaying against the same structure with changed parameters is spelled as `init!` of the modified model under the authored condition, then `replay!(sim, trc; restore = false)`.
- V232 The trace is not self-sufficient for it.
- V233 Its checkpoint holds the recording model's state after boundary zero, so the authored condition comes from outside.
- V234 The default form restores that state instead.
- V235 Structural mismatch is an error, and parametric difference is not.
- V236 ---
